summary: Assigns instruction codes and defines object formats and meanings for use with the HEMS Monitoring and Control Language of RFC 1023. It is described as provisional, so definitions could change. Readers are asked to confirm with the authors that they have the latest version.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1024 defines names, formats and meanings for instructions and values in the HEMS management system. Its authors explicitly describe the definitions as provisional and open to change.

subtitle: The provisional object and instruction definitions for the HEMS monitoring language.

tldr.problem: HEMS applications and managed entities need shared meanings and formats for instructions and the values that an entity exposes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1024 assigns ASN.1 tags, external formats and semantics to HEMS operations and objects, including a tree of dictionaries for system and network information.
tldr.outcome: The memo calls its definitions provisional and says they are subject to change. It is intended to be read with the HEMS language in RFC 1023.

facts.label: Counter rollover recommendation
facts.value: No more than once every 24 hours

sections.title: What the Memo Defines
sections.content:
The High-Level Entity Management System (HEMS) lets applications read and write values in remote entities that support a query processor. RFC 1024 defines the instruction codes, readable or writable objects and meanings of constants used by the HEMS Monitoring and Control Language.

For each value, the memo assigns an ASN.1 tag, an external representation such as INTEGER or OCTETSTRING, and a definition of what the value means. It says the definitions are provisional.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo gives shared names and meanings to values that HEMS applications can request. Its authors say the definitions may change.

sections.title: Instructions and Message Data
sections.content:
HEMS values are carried in the data sections of HEMP messages. Requests contain operations and operands, replies contain retrieved objects, and events contain an event object followed by related objects.

Operations and operands use postfix order: operands appear before the operation that uses them. The query processor pushes operands onto a stack and processes them when it reaches the operation code.
sections.plainLanguage: A HEMS request carries values and an instruction in a defined order. The instruction follows the values it acts on.

sections.title: Objects and the Root Dictionary
sections.content:
HEMS organizes objects in a tree-shaped type space with required and optional portions. An implementation is expected to support the required objects and relevant optional objects for its kind of entity.

The RootDictionary groups information in dictionaries for system variables, interfaces, the IP network layer, routing, transport protocols and applications. EventControls and IpApplications are optional. Values include counters, clock data and other information that an entity already stores or calculates.
sections.plainLanguage: HEMS groups information in a tree of dictionaries. The root groups contain system, interface, IP, routing and transport information, with some optional groups.

sections.title: Attributes, Counters and Errors
sections.content:
An application can request an object's attributes to learn its ASN.1 tag and underlying format. Attributes may also provide a description, label, units, precision or properties. Every Counter has a precision that identifies its rollover value.

The memo defines shared types including Counter, Histogram, TrafficMatrix, IpAddress and clocks. An Error object reports an error code, the position in the query where it was detected and a description. The RFC says a Counter should not roll over more than once in 24 hours.
sections.plainLanguage: Object attributes tell an application what a value represents and how it is encoded. A Counter records a number and has a defined point where it returns to zero.

sections.title: Limits on Changing Shared Values
sections.content:
HEMS is designed to allow more than one management application to query an entity. For that reason, the RFC says the SET operation cannot be applied to a Counter because changing it could interfere with another application's measurements.

The memo says HEMS does not provide protection from conflicting SET requests. It suggests that owned objects could be considered if such protection becomes necessary.
sections.plainLanguage: Several applications may read the same entity. Changing a shared counter could disrupt another application's measurements, and the memo does not define a general conflict-prevention mechanism.
